newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-BT backs MCI as Q1 profits edge up.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BT backs MCI as Q1 profits edge up.

text.p: British Telecommunications Plc on Thursday threw its considerable weight behind the plans of its American partner MCI despite the long-distance carrier's unexpectedly hefty loss forecast.

But BT, which earlier beat forecasts with a modest 1.4 percent rise in first quarter pre-tax profits to 881 million pounds ($1.4 billion), said it would only comment on a crucial business review of MCI Communication Corp when it could "see the way forward".

Finance director Robert Brace confirmed that the review, led by top BT and MCI executives after MCI's profit warning three weeks ago rocked a planned $20 billion transatlantic merger between the two companies, was likely to take weeks rather than months.
On Thursday's news, BT's shares slid further. The stock added another 7.5 pence loss to recent falls and was trading around 423p at 0900 GMT amid uncertainty over the future of the MCI merger.

"The results were ahead of expectations and that had to do with lower costs in some segments," said one analyst. "That's good and in a normal world the stock would be better, but we're not living in a normal world. These numbers are incidental to the bigger picture.

MCI surprised and disappointed BT -- and sparked calls for the merger to be re-negotiated or even abandoned -- by forecasting losses of $800 million this year and more next year because of delays breaking into the lucrative $100 billion local U.S. phone markets.

In what has been called by analysts typical "gung-ho" fashion, MCI decided to throw money at the problem by stepping up investments despite what it calls the foot-dragging by monopolistic local U.S. operators and the slow pace of U.S. local telephone deregulation efforts.
But Brace said BT backed the local investment plans of MCI, which on Wednesday reported a 6.7 percent drop in second quarter net income to $280 million.

"I think BT is very supportive of MCI and its attempts to develop business in the local (market) and in its calls for the regulators to open up markets...which are basically closed to competition," he said.

But it remains unclear whether BT will demand that MCI reins in its local capital expenditure programme with which it hopes to offset increasingly competitive international and long-distance telephone prices.

As some institutional investors grow increasingly irritated by a perceived news blackout ahead of the review's completion, Brace emphasised the complexity of analysing facts and determining the best way forward.
"It isn't a question of checking the books as such. It's a question of taking a view on what is likely to happen going forward," he said.
Brace said the company didn't "want to get sucked into any specific comments".
"We're happy to tell people what we have done when we have done it...we don't want to keep talking about it in the meantime."

BT, which is looking abroad to help boost growth amid rising competition from cable companies at home, has been caught between institutional investors who want a new deal to take into account lower earnings from MCI and between U.S. arbitrageurs who want terms unchanged to save them from multi-billion dollar losses.
BT's first quarter pre-tax profits were flattered by a lower-than-expected redundancy charge of 16 million pounds and a 20 million pound exceptional profit on sales.

But the group said rising competition at home, the start-up costs of European joint ventures ahead of European liberalisation next year and a lower contribution from MCI of 35 million pounds, all helped to keep a lid on profits.
Turnover from inland telephone calls was virtually static at 1.23 billion pounds and volume growth was offset almost entirely by over 200 million pounds of price cuts.
However, both inland and international call volume growth over a 12 month period rose to eight percent from around seven percent, BT said. ($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
